entry.title: Two mannequins flew around the Moon, and only one wore a vest 🌙

media:group.media:title: Two mannequins flew around the Moon, and only one wore a vest 🌙
media:group.media:description:
Helga and Zohar flew on Artemis I in 2022 to measure radiation beyond Earth’s protection. Helga went without a vest, while Zohar wore the AstroRad vest.
Now we know what a difference it could make. In a strong solar storm like the one in August 1972, the vest could cut an astronaut’s radiation dose by almost 60%.
#ESA #Artemis #SpaceRadiation

entry.title: What makes our experts dedicate their work lives to asteroids? 🪨🛰️

media:group.media:title: What makes our experts dedicate their work lives to asteroids? 🪨🛰️
media:group.media:description:
For some, it starts with a childhood fascination. For others, it’s the thrill of exploring the unknown. Our Hera engineers tell us what keeps them fascinated by these cosmic neighbours.
In November, Hera will finally reach the Didymos asteroid system to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s DART mission, which intentionally impacted Didymos’ moon, Dimorphos, in 2022 to test whether humanity could deflect an asteroid threatening Earth.
While the first close-up images of Didymos are expected earlier in the month, 25 November marks a particularly special moment: the first close-up look at Dimorphos.
After years of preparing for this moment, even Ian and Ingo can’t wait to discover what’s waiting out there. How do you think it will look like? 👀
#ESA #Satellite #HeraMission

media:group.media:title: Welcome home, Sophie Adenot
media:group.media:description:
After 237 days and over 3,700 orbits around Earth aboard the International Space Station, Sophie Adenot is back on Earth!
Following a handover to Crew-13, Sophie and her Crew-12 crewmates undocked on 7 October and splashed down off the coast of California the next day.
Now back in Europe, Sophie will begin her post-flight data collection and rehabilitation while readjusting to life on Earth after the longest mission in space by a European astronaut so far.
Welcome home, Sophie!
Credits: European Space Agency (ESA)

entry.title: Preparing Rosalind Franklin rover for a first drive on Mars

media:group.media:title: Preparing Rosalind Franklin rover for a first drive on Mars
media:group.media:description:
Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars, it has to get off its lander.
Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps.
In 2030, Rosalind Franklin will make this journey for real on Mars.
Credits: European Space Agency (ESA)

entry.title: Sophie Adenot's return to Earth - Statement from Cologne Airport

media:group.media:title: Sophie Adenot's return to Earth - Statement from Cologne Airport
media:group.media:description:
ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot has arrived back in Europe, landing in Cologne, Germany, two days after splashing down off the coast of California with her Crew-12 crewmates, following 237 days, nearly eight months, aboard the International Space Station for her εpsilon mission.
From Ellington Field in Houston, Sophie boarded a French Air and Space Force Airbus A330 MRTT Phénix bound for ESA’s European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany. She landed at 04:21 GMT/06:21 CEST on 10 October and was warmly welcomed on the apron by family, friends, colleagues, journalists and representatives from ESA Member States. She gave a short speech before answering questions from journalists.
Sophie will spend the next two to three weeks adjusting to Earth’s gravity and undergoing data collections at :envihab, a German Aerospace Center (DLR) facility located next to EAC. DLR teams work closely with ESA, providing operational, medical and scientific expertise to support astronauts’ return, recovery and readaptation to life on Earth. Sophie will then continue her rehabilitation and follow-up activities with the EAC training team.
Credits: European Space Agency (ESA)

entry.title: The space detectives arrive | The Incredible Adventures of the Hera Mission

media:group.media:title: The space detectives arrive | The Incredible Adventures of the Hera Mission
media:group.media:description:
Meet Hera, our very own asteroid detective. Together with two CubeSats – Milani the rock decoder and Juventas the radar visionary – Hera is off on an adventure to explore Didymos, a double asteroid system that is typical of the thousands that pose an impact risk to planet Earth.
After their two year cosmic roadtrip, Hera and its little CubeSat companions have finally arrived at Didymos and Dimorphos – the very first Solar System object to have had its orbit shifted by human action. Suitable for kids and adults alike, this episode of ‘The Incredible Adventures of the Hera mission’ explains what ESA’s asteroid detective and its CubeSat assistants will be up to once they arrive, and precisely how they are going to say goodbye to each other – letting the CubeSats begin their close-up exam of this historic space rock.
